appraisal_events.evidence: "il a gâché un joli tempérament de peintre... Au fond c'était un médiocre... il était d'un sale... j'appelle cela du barbouillé, c'est d'un poncif, et puis ça manque de relief, de personnalité" alongside her rêverie over his painted roses, "où se trouvaient résumés... son grand talent... leur longue amitié."
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Verdurin publicly disparages Elstir's current work, character, and cleanliness at length, even as she privately, wistfully lingers on the talent and intimacy she once possessed a claim to; the narrator frames this self-serving contradiction with quiet irony.

appraisal_events.evidence: "« Gare », dit à mi-voix Mme Verdurin en montrant Brichot"; "Il manque évidemment d'originalité et de goût, il a une terrible mémoire... Brichot sait tout, et nous jette à la tête, pendant le dîner, des piles de dictionnaires"; "ses paroles ne portaient plus, avaient à vaincre un silence hostile"; his disgrace with Mme Verdurin is one "qu'il savait définitive."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator recounts Brichot's durable fall from favor within the Verdurin 'petit clan': his once-prized erudition now meets private mockery and a hostile silence, a settled decline distinct from the still-unfolding dinner-table humiliation of Saniette.

appraisal_events.evidence: His admiring remarks about the shabby, unfashionable details of the Raspelière repeatedly misfire ("J'indignai Mme de Cambremer," "Mon éloge... n'eut pas plus de succès"), until "Cette fois Mme de Cambremer me tourna résolument le dos."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator, staged as a participant rather than merely a lens, is visibly and physically rebuffed by Mme de Cambremer after his sincere but socially maladroit enthusiasm displeases her; this pairs with Mme Verdurin's private view that his admiration for Brichot marks him as an outsider to the clan.

status_effects.explanation: Elstir is publicly disparaged by Mme Verdurin as mediocre and tasteless in his current work, a net negative framing softened only by her private, wistful admiration for his earlier talent.
Brichot's standing within the Verdurin salon has durably declined into private mockery and a cooling reception, described by the narrator as a settled, not passing, disgrace.
The narrator, as an in-scene participant, is treated as an outsider this evening: physically rebuffed by Mme de Cambremer and privately judged unsophisticated by Mme Verdurin.
